In [[mathematics]], the '''measurable Riemann mapping theorem''' is a theorem proved in 1960 by [[Lars Ahlfors]] and [[Lipman Bers]]<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Riemann's Mapping Theorem for Variable Metrics|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1970141?origin=crossref|journal=The Annals of Mathematics|date=September 1960|pages=385|volume=72|issue=2|doi=10.2307/1970141|first=Lars|last=Ahlfors|first2=Lipman|last2=Bers|url-access=subscription}}</ref> in [[complex analysis]] and [[geometric function theory]]. Contrary to its name, it is not a direct generalization of the [[Riemann mapping theorem]], but instead a result concerning [[quasiconformal mapping]]s and solutions of the [[Beltrami equation]]. The result was prefigured by earlier results of [[Charles Morrey]] from 1938 on quasi-linear [[elliptic partial differential equation]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=On the Solutions of Quasi-Linear Elliptic Partial Differential Equations|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1989904?origin=crossref|journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society|date=January 1938|pages=126|volume=43|issue=1|doi=10.2307/1989904|first=Charles B.|last=Morrey}}</ref>

== Theorem ==
The theorem of Ahlfors and Bers states that if μ is a bounded measurable function on '''C''' with <math>\|\mu\|_\infty < 1</math>, then there is a unique solution ''f'' of the Beltrami equation

:<math> \partial_{\overline{z}} f(z) = \mu(z) \partial_z f(z)</math>

for which ''f'' is a quasiconformal homeomorphism of '''C''' fixing the points 0, 1 and ∞. A similar result is true with '''C''' replaced by the [[unit disk]] '''D'''. Their proof used the [[Beurling transform]], a [[singular integral operator]].
